categories.name: Payer mix strategy
categories.summary: Which payers the practice's revenue comes from, what each pays per visit, how fast and how reliably. Payer mix is partly a choice: which plans to join, which to leave, and which patients and sites to pursue.
good_looks_like: Revenue, visits and payment per visit are reported by payer class every quarter.
The practice knows its three best and three worst payers by net payment per visit and by denial rate.
Dependence on any one payer is known and planned for.
Decisions to join or leave a plan are made from numbers.
failure_modes: The practice joins every plan offered and never checks which ones pay less than the cost of the visit.
One payer provides most of the revenue and its yearly rate change is never modeled.
A plan's low rate is tolerated because nobody added up its denials and delays too.
Payer mix shifts toward slower, lower-paying plans without anyone noticing.
key_questions: What share of revenue comes from each payer class?
What do we collect per visit from each payer, after denials?
Which plan would we drop if we could, and what would it cost us?
How has the mix changed in two years?

actions.action: Report by payer every quarter
actions.detail: Charges, payments, visits, payment per visit, denial rate and days to pay.

actions.action: Rank payers by what each really pays per visit
actions.detail: Payment per visit after denials and write-offs, beside the staff time each payer takes.

actions.action: Model the largest payer's rate change
actions.detail: Each November for Medicare, when the final fee schedule rule comes out, and at each contract renewal for plans.

actions.action: Decide yearly on each small plan
actions.detail: Keep, renegotiate or leave, with the access consequences for patients and sites.

categories.applies_when: Every practice, and most of all practices serving older adults, which live on Medicare and Medicare Advantage and mostly choose which plans to contract with. For facility-based practices the mix comes with the buildings served: residents arrive with their coverage, so decide by facility and plan.

vendor_refs.note: Adds tracking each payer's share of visits beside its share of revenue. Its 25% single-payer alarm and its pay bands by payer class cite no source.
Claims 55% to 75% of geriatric patients are in Medicare Advantage, with no source. Wrongly says those plans need not follow Medicare's coverage rules.

categories.evidence_note: Management practice. Denial rates by payer type are measured in peer-reviewed studies: Medicare Advantage 17% of first claims (2019), Medicaid fee-for-service 17.8 points above Medicare (2013 to 2015). No benchmark for an ideal mix exists.

metrics.name: Share of revenue from the largest payer
metrics.definition: Payments from the single largest payer, with its patients' cost sharing, as a share of all payments received.
metrics.formula: Largest payer's payments / total payments from all payers and patients
metrics.benchmark_note: Not a target. American Medical Association survey, 2016 data: physicians' patients averaged 43% commercial, 29% Medicare and 17% Medicaid. KFF: 55% of eligible Medicare beneficiaries were in Medicare Advantage in 2026. Above half on one payer, model its rate changes yearly.
metrics.data_hint: Payments by payer from the billing system.
metrics.vendor_claim: The purchased library calls any payer above 25% of net revenue a concentration risk.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Unverifiable. No source is given. A practice serving older adults passes 25% on Medicare by design, so the alarm would never clear.

metrics.name: Net revenue per visit by payer
metrics.definition: Payments received from a payer, including its patients' cost sharing collected, divided by visits billed to that payer.
metrics.formula: Payments for the payer's patients / visits billed to that payer
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found, because the figure depends on the mix of codes billed. Compare with your own trend. Compare payers with each other and with Medicare's allowed amount for the same codes.

categories.name: Contract inventory and terms
categories.summary: Holding a signed copy of every payer agreement and its current fee schedule, and knowing the terms that cost money when missed: filing and appeal deadlines, amendment rules, renewal and termination dates.
good_looks_like: One folder holds every payer contract, amendment and fee schedule.
A register lists each contract's effective date, renewal date, notice period, filing limit and appeal deadline.
Fee schedules are loaded where payments can be checked against them.
Payer notices of amendment are read and answered before their deadline.
Staff know the notice rules. In Florida, a health maintenance organization owes 30 days' written notice of payment schedule changes and 60 days' notice before ending a contract without cause.
failure_modes: The practice cannot find its contract, so it cannot dispute an underpayment in time. In Florida the limit is 12 months after the payment for state-regulated plans.
A plan changes rates by a mailed or posted notice that takes effect unless the practice objects within the contract's window, and nobody reads it.
A contract renews automatically for years at an old rate.
Filing limits differ by payer (12 months for Original Medicare, 6 months for Florida-regulated plans, contract terms for Medicare Advantage) and staff apply one rule to all.
key_questions: Do we hold a signed contract and current fee schedule for every plan we bill?
What is each plan's filing limit and appeal deadline?
Which contracts renew or can be reopened in the next 12 months?
Who reads payer notices, and how fast?

actions.action: Collect every contract and fee schedule
actions.detail: Request missing copies from each plan's provider relations or network office.

actions.action: Build the contract register
actions.detail: Dates, notice periods, filing and appeal limits, amendment clause, contact, and plan type (state-regulated, employer self-funded, Medicare Advantage, Medicaid), since different laws apply to each.

actions.action: Load fee schedules into the billing system
actions.detail: So that each payment can be compared with the expected amount.

actions.action: Log and answer payer notices
actions.detail: Record the date received and the reply deadline for every amendment or policy notice, including those posted on plan websites. Object in writing while the window is open.

categories.applies_when: Every practice that contracts with health plans. Medicare fee-for-service has no negotiated contract, but its fee schedule should be loaded the same way.

vendor_refs.note: Adds a clause reading list and a contract register. Its typical state payment deadline, 30 to 45 days, is not Florida's 20. Omits that self-funded plans escape state law.
Adds a control for amendment notices: one owner, a dated log, calendared reply dates. Calls silent acceptance simply legal and cites no state or Medicare Advantage notice rule.

categories.evidence_note: Regulation and statute. Medicare Advantage plans must give written notice of material rule changes and 60 days' notice before ending a contract without cause (42 CFR 422.202). Florida examples: sections 627.6131, 641.3155 and 641.315. State laws usually do not reach employer self-funded plans.

metrics.name: Payers with a signed contract and current fee schedule on file
metrics.definition: Share of contracted payers for which the practice holds the signed agreement and the fee schedule now in force.
metrics.formula: Payers with contract and current fee schedule on file / contracted payers
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. The target from first principles is 100%.
metrics.data_hint: The contract register, checked against the list of payers billed in the last 12 months.

categories.name: Rate analysis and negotiation
categories.summary: Comparing what each plan pays with Medicare and with other plans for the practice's own most-used codes, and asking for better terms where the practice has something the plan needs.
good_looks_like: Each plan's rates for the practice's top codes are expressed as a percentage of Medicare's rate for the same locality and setting.
The practice knows what it offers each plan: access, quality results, coverage of sites the plan must serve.
Requests are made in writing, with data, well before renewal.
Terms other than rates are negotiated too: filing limits, appeal rights, amendment notice.
The practice knows what leaving a network would change. Outside a Medicare Advantage network, a clinician must accept Original Medicare's amount as payment in full (42 CFR 422.214).
failure_modes: A plan pays below Medicare and nobody has calculated it.
The practice asks for more with no data and accepts the first refusal.
A rate increase is won and never loaded, so underpayments go unnoticed.
Charges are set below a plan's allowed amount. Plans and Medicare pay the lesser of the charge or the fee schedule, so the practice caps its own payment.
Competing practices agree among themselves on the fees to ask of a plan. Fee agreements among competing physicians are price fixing, illegal in itself under federal antitrust law.
key_questions: For our top 15 codes, what does each plan pay as a percent of Medicare?
Which plan is furthest below the others?
What do we offer that a plan needs?
Are our charges above every plan's allowed amount?
Is each plan's rate tied to the current Medicare fee schedule or to an old year, and does it rise each year?

actions.action: Build a payer-by-code rate table
actions.detail: Top 15 codes by revenue: each plan's allowed amount (not the paid amount) from remittances, beside Medicare's rate for the same locality and setting.

actions.action: Write the case before asking
actions.detail: Volume, access, quality and cost results, the specific rates and yearly increase requested, and the point at which the practice would leave the network.

actions.action: Ask in writing well before renewal
actions.detail: Start before the contract's notice deadline for ending or not renewing, so a refusal still leaves a choice. Follow up on a schedule.

actions.action: Verify new rates are paid
actions.detail: Check the first month of remittances after any change.

actions.action: Look up what the plan pays others
actions.detail: Employer and individual-market plans must publish in-network rates in public data files (45 CFR 147.212). The files are huge, so use a lookup tool or an adviser. Medicare Advantage and Medicaid plan rates are not included.

categories.applies_when: Practices with commercial, Medicare Advantage or Medicaid managed care contracts. Small practices are paid less than large groups and have little power on rates, but can ask for better non-rate terms, and gain power where a plan needs their sites covered, such as nursing homes its members live in.

vendor_refs.note: Adds a negotiation timeline, a data package and replies to stock objections. Credits public price files to the wrong law. Its 15.5% average increase is a contracting vendor's own figure.
Adds the check that no charge sits below a contract rate. Its charge rule of 200% to 250% of Medicare has no source and ignores Medicare's limiting charge.

categories.evidence_note: Method is professional practice. Measured averages: commercial preferred provider plans paid 147% of Medicare for clinician services in 2024 (Medicare Payment Advisory Commission, MedPAC), Medicaid 75% (KFF). Commercial in-network rates are public by federal rule since 2022. The antitrust rule is Supreme Court precedent.

metrics.name: Contracted rates as a percent of Medicare, by payer
metrics.definition: For the practice's main codes, each plan's allowed amount divided by Medicare's allowed amount for the same code, locality and place of service.
metrics.formula: Plan allowed amount / Medicare allowed amount, weighted by the practice's code volume
metrics.benchmark_typical: commercial about 147%, Medicare Advantage about 97%, Medicaid about 75% of Medicare
metrics.benchmark_note: Measured averages, not targets. MedPAC, 2024: commercial preferred provider plans 147% of Medicare, from 124% for care management visits to 213% for CT scans. A 2017 study of 2007 to 2012 claims: Medicare Advantage 97% for an office visit. KFF, 2024: Medicaid 75% (Florida 64%).
metrics.data_hint: Fee schedules or allowed amounts on remittances, against the Medicare fee schedule lookup.
metrics.vendor_claim: The purchased library gives bands with no source: commercial plans 110% to 145% of Medicare, Medicare Advantage 85% to 110%, Medicaid 50% to 80%.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Partly supported. Measured averages sit in or near the bands (147%, 97%, 75%), but nothing is cited and a national band says little about one practice's codes.

categories.name: Credentialing and enrollment
categories.summary: Getting each clinician enrolled with Medicare, Medicaid and every plan, at every location, before they see patients, and keeping those enrollments current. Most payers pay only for services on or after the enrollment effective date.
good_looks_like: A tracker lists every clinician, payer and location with status, effective date and next revalidation or recredentialing date, plus hospital privileges and their renewal dates.
Plan applications start when a clinician's offer is signed. The Medicare application is filed no more than 60 days before the start date, because earlier ones can be returned.
Revalidation and recredentialing requests are answered well before the deadline.
Changes of location, ownership or clinicians are reported within the required time, including each new facility where patients are seen.
The shared credentialing profile that health plans draw on (the CAQH Provider Data Portal) is re-attested every 120 days.
failure_modes: A clinician sees patients for months before an application is filed. Medicare looks back 30 days at most and some plans not at all, so the visits go unpaid.
A recredentialing letter goes to an old address and the plan terminates the practice.
A new office or facility is never added to the Medicare enrollment record, though a new practice location must be reported within 30 days.
The clinician's National Provider Identifier record lists an old specialty or address. Changes must be reported to the national registry within 30 days.
A clinician who bills Medicare nothing for six months, or misses a revalidation, may be deactivated. Medicare pays nothing for services given while deactivated.
key_questions: Is every clinician enrolled and current with every payer we bill?
When is each next revalidation or recredentialing due?
How many claims were denied last quarter for enrollment reasons?
Are our national provider records and practice locations up to date?

actions.action: Keep one enrollment tracker
actions.detail: Clinician, payer, location, status, effective date, next due date, last contact.

actions.action: File early and follow up weekly
actions.detail: Start plan applications at offer acceptance. File with Medicare within the 60 days before the start date. Billing starts on the later of filing date or first service, with at most a 30-day look-back (42 CFR 424.520 to 424.526).

actions.action: Calendar every renewal date
actions.detail: Medicare revalidation every 5 years (due dates are posted seven months ahead, no extensions), plan recredentialing at least every 3 years, Medicaid at least every 5, the CAQH profile every 120 days, and hospital privileges on each hospital's cycle.

actions.action: Report changes on time
actions.detail: Medicare requires reports of ownership changes, adverse legal actions and added, changed or closed practice locations within 30 days, and all other changes within 90 (42 CFR 424.516).

actions.action: Reassign each clinician's Medicare payment to the practice
actions.detail: Each clinician enrolls individually and reassigns payment to the group on the same application (form CMS-855I, or online). The separate reassignment form was discontinued.

categories.applies_when: Every practice that bills insurers: each clinician needs separate enrollment with Medicare, with Medicaid where dual-eligible patients are seen, and with each plan. Facility-based practices list each hospital, nursing facility or assisted living community as a Medicare practice location, and home-visit practices state that care is given in patients' homes.

vendor_refs.note: Adds a clinician-by-payer calendar with early triggers and a status tracker. Says to file with Medicare 90 days ahead, though an application over 60 days early can be returned.
Adds an enrollment order for a new practice. Says Medicare may be filed only 30 days ahead (the rule is 60) and names the discontinued reassignment form.

categories.evidence_note: Medicare's rules are federal regulation, and its contractor publishes processing standards. Medicare Advantage plans must recredential at least every 3 years (42 CFR 422.204). Plans publish no processing times. Medical Group Management Association (MGMA) poll, 2021: waits up to 100 days.

metrics.name: Clinician and payer pairs that are active and current
metrics.definition: Share of clinician-payer-location combinations the practice bills that are enrolled, effective and not past a revalidation date.
metrics.formula: Active and current enrollments / enrollments the practice needs
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. The target from first principles is 100%.

metrics.name: Days from application to approval
metrics.definition: Calendar days from submitting a complete enrollment application to the payer's approval, when claims for that clinician can first be sent.
metrics.formula: Approval date - complete application date, by payer
metrics.benchmark_best: 15 days for a clean online Medicare application
metrics.benchmark_note: First Coast (Medicare's Florida contractor) processing standards, 2026: 95% of clean online applications in 15 days, all within 50, and 50 to 85 days when more information is needed. Plans publish no standards. MGMA members reported waits of up to 100 days (2021).
metrics.data_hint: The enrollment tracker: application and approval dates for each clinician and payer.
metrics.vendor_claim: All priority payers approved within 120 days of application, with escalation at 90 days. Medicare typically takes 30 to 45 days.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Unverifiable for plans, which publish no standards. For Medicare the contractor's own standard is faster: 15 days for most clean online applications.

metrics.name: Denials for enrollment or credentialing
metrics.definition: Share of claims denied because the rendering or billing clinician was not enrolled or eligible with the payer on the date of service.
metrics.formula: Claims denied for provider enrollment reasons / claims adjudicated
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. These denials are preventable, so the target is zero. MGMA poll, August 2021 (425 practices): 54% saw credentialing denials rising.
metrics.data_hint: Remittance reason codes 185, B7, 208 and 242: clinician not eligible, not certified on the date of service, identifier not matched, not a network provider.
metrics.vendor_claim: Target 0%: the library treats every credentialing denial as a preventable lapse.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Supported as a first-principles target. No published benchmark exists.

categories.name: Medicare fee-for-service rules and the annual fee schedule
categories.summary: How Original Medicare pays: a national fee schedule set each year, adjusted by locality and by whether the service was given in a facility. Each November's final rule changes what the practice will be paid from January.
good_looks_like: Someone reads the summary of the final rule each November and lists what changes for the practice's codes.
The top codes are repriced at next year's rates before the year starts.
The practice knows whether each service is paid at the facility or non-facility rate, and why.
Participation status is a deliberate choice, reviewed between mid-November and December 31, when Medicare allows changes.
Staff know the standing cuts: 2% off Medicare's share (sequestration), and 85% of the physician rate when a nurse practitioner or physician assistant bills under their own number.
failure_modes: The conversion factor falls and the practice learns it from its January deposits.
A place-of-service error pays the wrong rate for years. When the higher rate was paid in error, the difference is an overpayment that must be returned.
A code is deleted or replaced on January 1 and claims are rejected for weeks. Example: in 2027 the visit complexity add-on G2211 becomes a modifier.
Budgeting assumes last year's rates.
key_questions: What does next year's final rule do to our top 15 codes?
Which of our services are paid at the facility rate?
Have deleted, new or revised codes been loaded for January?
Are we a participating provider, and do we know what that means?

actions.action: Read the final rule summary each November
actions.detail: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) publishes a fact sheet. Note the conversion factor and any policy touching the practice's services.

actions.action: Reprice the top codes
actions.detail: Next year's rate by code, locality and place of service, times this year's volume. CMS posts the new values with the final rule.

actions.action: Load code changes before January 1
actions.detail: New, deleted and revised codes and any modifier changes.

actions.action: Check place of service on a sample
actions.detail: Facility and non-facility rates can differ by a third for care management codes. Nursing facility visits paid less in a Part A skilled stay (place of service 31) during 2026 and pay the same from 2027.

actions.action: Decide Medicare participation each year
actions.detail: A non-participating clinician is paid 5% less and may charge patients no more than 115% of that reduced amount (42 CFR 414.48). Changes are allowed from mid-November to December 31.

categories.applies_when: Every practice that bills Original Medicare. The effect of each year's rule depends on code mix and setting: the 2026 rule cut practice expense payment for services in facilities, and the 2027 rule restores equal payment for nursing facility visits whether or not the patient is in a Part A stay.

vendor_refs.note: Gives the 2026 conversion factors correctly and a yearly update cycle. Counts only hospital outpatient and surgery centers as facility settings, missing skilled nursing stays, and omits the limiting charge.
Treats Traditional Medicare as stable from year to year. The 2026 and 2027 rules changed conversion factors, facility payment and how the visit add-on is billed.

categories.evidence_note: The fee schedule and its yearly changes are federal rulemaking. 2026 conversion factors: $33.40, and $33.57 for qualifying alternative payment model participants. 2027: $32.63 (down 2.31%) and $32.95 (down 1.83%), because a one-year 2.5% increase ends.

metrics.name: Estimated revenue effect of the coming year's Medicare fee schedule
metrics.definition: Change in yearly Medicare revenue expected from the next fee schedule, holding volume and code mix constant.
metrics.formula: Sum over codes of (next year's rate - this year's rate) x this year's volume
metrics.benchmark_note: Not a target. For 2027 the conversion factor falls 2.31% for most clinicians and 1.83% for qualifying alternative payment model participants (CMS final rule, November 2026). Code and setting changes add to or offset that, so reprice your own codes.
metrics.data_hint: Volume by code and place of service from the billing system, with the Medicare fee schedule lookup for both years.

categories.name: Medicare Advantage operations
categories.summary: Working with private Medicare plans: confirming network status, meeting each plan's authorization and referral rules, tracking payment timing and denials, and disputing denials. Each plan is a separate set of rules.
good_looks_like: A one-page sheet per plan lists network status, authorization and referral rules, filing limit, dispute process and contacts.
Enrollment in a plan is confirmed monthly for continuing patients.
Denials are tracked by plan and disputed through the contract's process.
The practice knows what happens to billing when a plan member elects hospice.
Staff know the federal rules plans must follow: Medicare's national and local coverage rules apply, and a service approved in advance cannot later be denied as not medically necessary.
failure_modes: Staff assume a plan works like Original Medicare and miss its authorization, referral, network and filing rules.
A patient switches plans and the practice bills the old one for months.
Denials are written off, although 57% of Medicare Advantage claim denials were later overturned in a study of 2019 claims.
Claims for a plan member on hospice keep going to the plan.
Staff give a plan member Original Medicare's advance notice of non-coverage. Contracted clinicians may not use that form for plan members. Ask the plan for a coverage decision instead.
key_questions: For each plan, are we in network, and what needs authorization or a referral?
What is each plan's denial rate and average days to pay?
How many denials did we dispute last quarter, and how many did we win?
Do we re-check plan enrollment every month?
Does any plan contract carry a bonus or shared-savings addendum, and who tracks what it requires?

actions.action: Write a one-page sheet per plan
actions.detail: Network status, product types, authorization and referral rules, filing and dispute deadlines, contacts. Out of network, covered services are paid at no less than Original Medicare's amount, which the clinician must accept as payment in full.

actions.action: Track denials and days to pay by plan
actions.detail: Monthly, beside Original Medicare for comparison. Also log authorization requests: since 2026 plans must answer a standard request within 7 calendar days (42 CFR 422.568).

actions.action: Dispute denials systematically
actions.detail: Use the contract's dispute process. Cite the rules: plans must follow Medicare's national and local coverage decisions (42 CFR 422.101) and may not deny an approved service later for medical necessity (42 CFR 422.138).

actions.action: Handle hospice elections
actions.detail: From the election date Original Medicare, not the plan, pays. Professional claims need modifier GV (attending physician not employed by the hospice) or GW (unrelated to the terminal illness).

actions.action: Re-check plan enrollment at the start of each month
actions.detail: Nursing facility residents staying 90 days or more may change plans at any time, and people with both Medicare and Medicaid once a month. Check plan, hospice status and Medicaid status together.

categories.applies_when: Any practice with Medicare patients: more than half of eligible beneficiaries (55% in 2026) are in these plans. Facility-based practices face more switching, since long-stay nursing facility residents may change plans at any time and people with both Medicare and Medicaid monthly, so enrollment is re-checked every month.

vendor_refs.note: Adds a per-plan rule inventory and claim checkpoints. Wrongly says a plan may recoup for medical necessity after approving the service, and presents the patient's appeal ladder as the practice's.
Adds plan-by-plan protocols for the largest plans. Wrongly says plans need not follow Medicare's rules and tells staff to use Original Medicare's advance notice form for plan members.

categories.evidence_note: Denial and overturn rates are from a peer-reviewed study of 2019 claims and from KFF's analysis of 2024 plan data. Federal rules, not state prompt-payment laws, govern these plans. Contracted clinicians dispute payment under the contract. The federal appeal path belongs to the patient.

metrics.name: Medicare Advantage initial denial rate
metrics.definition: Share of claims to Medicare Advantage plans that are denied on first adjudication, reported by plan.
metrics.formula: Medicare Advantage claims denied on first adjudication / Medicare Advantage claims adjudicated
metrics.benchmark_note: Health Affairs, 2025, using 2019 claims from plans covering 30% of the market: 17% of first claims denied, and 57% of denials later overturned. Measured, not a target. Set targets by plan, not as one blended figure.
metrics.vendor_claim: The purchased library sets a dashboard target of under 6% for the Medicare Advantage denial rate.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Unverifiable as a target, and far below the one large measurement (17% of first claims in 2019). No source is given.

metrics.name: Share of revenue from Medicare Advantage
metrics.definition: Payments from Medicare Advantage plans as a share of total payments.
metrics.benchmark_note: Not a target. A rising share means more revenue depends on contracts, authorization rules and dispute work. For context, 55% of eligible Medicare beneficiaries were in these plans in 2026 (KFF).

categories.name: Medicaid and dual-eligible rules
categories.summary: The rules for patients who have Medicaid, alone or alongside Medicare. They decide whether any secondary payment arrives, whether the patient may be billed, and which managed care plan is responsible.
good_looks_like: Every clinician who sees dual-eligible patients (those with both Medicare and Medicaid) is enrolled with the state Medicaid program.
Staff know that Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries, a low-income Medicaid group, may not be billed Medicare cost sharing, even when Medicaid pays nothing and even in a Medicare Advantage plan.
For protected patients, coinsurance that Medicaid will not pay is posted as a contractual adjustment, not left as a balance.
The practice knows each Medicaid managed care plan's filing limit and payment method.
failure_modes: A clinician is not enrolled with Medicaid, so the claims Medicare passes on to Medicaid (crossover claims) are rejected and nothing is paid.
Patients protected by federal law receive statements for coinsurance. Money collected must be refunded, and the practice risks sanctions.
Uncollectible dual-eligible balances inflate receivables for years.
A Medicaid plan's short filing limit is missed.
Staff treat every patient with Medicaid as protected, or none. The federal ban names Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries. For other categories, check the eligibility answer and state rules first.
key_questions: Are all our clinicians enrolled with Medicaid?
What share of our Medicare patients also have Medicaid?
How much secondary payment do we actually receive on those patients?
Are protected patients flagged so they never get a statement?

actions.action: Enroll every clinician with Medicaid
actions.detail: States must let Medicare-enrolled clinicians enroll so cost-sharing claims can be processed (42 CFR 455.410). Revalidation comes at least every 5 years. In Florida, enrollment takes effect the day the agency receives the application.

actions.action: Flag protected patients
actions.detail: Identify Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries from the eligibility answer and suppress statements.

actions.action: Post unpayable coinsurance as contractual
actions.detail: Use a specific adjustment code so it can be reported separately.

actions.action: Know each Medicaid plan's rules
actions.detail: Filing limit, crossover handling and whether it pays electronically. Federal rules cap a state program's filing limit at 12 months from service (42 CFR 447.45). States and managed care plans may set shorter limits, such as 180 days.

categories.applies_when: Practices serving low-income older or disabled patients, including most nursing facility practices, since 11% of dual-eligible people live in an institution against 2% of other Medicare beneficiaries. State rules differ: in Florida, Medicaid pays nothing on Medicare coinsurance when Medicare's payment already meets Medicaid's own rate, and long-term care is paid through managed care plans.

vendor_refs.note: Adds the reminder that Medicaid's payment, often zero, settles a protected patient's claim. Stretches the billing ban to every dual-eligible patient and says Medicare is always primary.

categories.evidence_note: The billing ban for Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries is federal law, even when Medicaid pays nothing. State crossover rules vary: 41 states pay only up to the Medicaid rate for physician services (MACPAC, the federal Medicaid payment commission, May 2025).

metrics.name: Share of patients who are dual eligible
metrics.definition: Patients with both Medicare and Medicaid as a share of the practice's Medicare patients.
metrics.benchmark_note: Not a target. Federal payment commissions' data book (MedPAC and MACPAC), 2022 data: 20% of Medicare beneficiaries were dually eligible, and 11% of them lived in an institution. Medicare publishes each clinician's count for fee-for-service patients. More protected patients means more uncollectible coinsurance.
metrics.data_hint: Eligibility data, or Medicare's public file by clinician, which counts beneficiaries with both Medicare and Medicaid.

metrics.name: Secondary payment received on dual-eligible coinsurance
metrics.definition: Payments received from Medicaid on Medicare coinsurance and deductibles, as a share of the amounts crossed over.
metrics.formula: Medicaid crossover payments / Medicare cost sharing crossed over to Medicaid
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. Expect a low figure in the 41 states with lesser-of rules for physician services (MACPAC, May 2025). Its use is to confirm crossover claims are being processed at all.
metrics.data_hint: Secondary remittances from Medicaid against Medicare cost sharing.

categories.name: Payment policy monitoring
categories.summary: Watching for rule changes that alter what gets paid: Medicare's yearly rule, the regional contractor's coverage policies and review topics, plan policy bulletins and code updates. Each change should become a written rule in the billing process.
good_looks_like: One person is responsible for reading payer and contractor updates on a schedule.
Each relevant change is turned into a dated entry in the practice's billing rules.
The contractor's list of services under targeted review is checked against what the practice bills.
Code changes are loaded on their own calendars: procedure codes January 1, diagnosis codes October 1 (with an April update), and bundling edits each quarter.
failure_modes: The practice learns of a policy change from a wave of denials.
A contractor announces a review of a service the practice bills heavily and nobody sees it.
A rule is learned once and forgotten when staff change.
Plan bulletins go to an unread mailbox.
key_questions: Who reads Medicare contractor and plan updates, and how often?
Is any service we bill on the contractor's active review list?
Where are our billing rules written down, with dates?
How did we find out about the last policy change that affected us?

actions.action: Assign a monthly policy review
actions.detail: Contractor news, coverage policy changes, the review topic list, each plan's bulletins and Medicare's weekly newsletter for providers. Local coverage decisions are posted at least 45 days before they take effect, so a monthly check catches each one.

actions.action: Keep a dated rulebook
actions.detail: One entry per rule, with its source and the date it took effect.

actions.action: Check billed services against review topics
actions.detail: Medicare contractors post the services under targeted review, each marked active or inactive. If a high-volume service is listed, audit a sample before the contractor does.

actions.action: Subscribe to the contractor's and plans' notices
actions.detail: Sent to a mailbox someone reads.

actions.action: Load code updates on schedule
actions.detail: Procedure codes each January 1, diagnosis codes each October 1 and April 1, bundling edits each quarter. Confirm the billing system or its vendor has loaded each set.

categories.applies_when: Every practice, whatever the setting: what differs is the watch list, which for facility-based practices centers on visit codes, care management and place-of-service rules. Those using automated billing should treat each policy change as a change to the automation's rules, reviewed before release.

vendor_refs.note: Shows how to turn one rule change into desk routines. Applies the 2026 seven-day authorization deadline to all payers. It binds Medicare Advantage and Medicaid plans, and excludes drugs.
Adds a ready payer change log sheet for recording each policy change with its source and date. Its risk flags misfire on closed cases, so weekly counts overstate.

categories.evidence_note: Federal compliance guidance recommends reviewing policies at least once a year for changes in law and program requirements (Office of Inspector General, 2023). Contractors publish their review topics, and local coverage decisions carry 45 days' notice by statute, so monitoring is straightforward.

metrics.name: Payer policy review cadence
metrics.definition: How often a named person reviews Medicare contractor and plan policy updates and records the result.
metrics.formula: Count of documented policy reviews in the last 12 months
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. Federal compliance guidance asks for a policy review at least once a year. Monthly is a reasonable standard here, because local coverage decisions take effect at least 45 days after posting.

categories.name: Veterans, military, commercial and out-of-network payers
categories.summary: The smaller payers, each with its own gatekeeping: Veterans Affairs community care, the military health plan (TRICARE), workers' compensation, small commercial plans, and patients seen out of network or with no insurance.
good_looks_like: For each small payer the practice has decided to participate properly or not at all.
Veterans Affairs community care visits have an authorization on file before the service, and the claim goes where the referral says.
Self-pay and uninsured patients get a good-faith estimate for scheduled care, and out-of-network patients get the notices the law requires.
Write-offs for unenrolled payers are counted, so the cost of not enrolling is known.
Staff know Medicare is primary for patients who also have the military health plan, so those claims go to Medicare first.
failure_modes: A clinician sees patients from a payer that has never credentialed them, and every claim is written off.
Veterans' visits are billed with no authorization, or later than 180 days after the service, the limit set by federal law.
An out-of-network clinician at an in-network hospital bills a commercially insured patient beyond cost sharing. Federal law bans this, and hospitalists cannot use the consent exception.
Small-plan claims are abandoned because each needs a phone call.
A clinician with no Medicare Advantage contract bills a plan member more than Medicare allows. Non-contracted clinicians must accept Original Medicare's amount as payment in full.
key_questions: Which payers do we bill without being enrolled or contracted?
How much did we write off last year for those payers?
Do Veterans Affairs community care visits always have an authorization first?
Do we ever bill patients out of network, and do we give the required notices?

actions.action: List every payer billed without enrollment
actions.detail: With last year's charges and write-offs for each.

actions.action: Decide for each: enroll or stop
actions.detail: Enroll where volume justifies it. Veterans Affairs community care generally pays no more than Medicare's rate (38 CFR 17.4035). Otherwise refer or schedule those patients differently.

actions.action: Require authorization for veterans' community care
actions.detail: All non-urgent, non-emergency care needs Veterans Affairs approval in advance. Record the referral number before the visit, send the claim where the referral says, and file within 180 days.

actions.action: Give self-pay patients a good-faith estimate
actions.detail: Within 1 business day when care is scheduled at least 3 business days ahead, within 3 business days when scheduled at least 10 ahead or on request (45 CFR 149.610).

actions.action: Bill Medicare first for military health plan members
actions.detail: For a patient with both, Medicare is always primary. Claims to the military plan must be filed within one year of the service (32 CFR 199.7 and 199.8).

categories.applies_when: Practices with a scattering of patients outside their main payers. Federal surprise-billing rules cover out-of-network care at hospitals and surgery centers for commercially insured patients, so they bind hospital-based clinicians but not visits in nursing facilities, assisted living or the home, while the estimate duty for self-pay patients applies everywhere.

vendor_refs.note: Adds a workflow for disputing out-of-network payments from commercial plans. Tells readers to price offers against Medicare rates, which the arbitrator may not consider (45 CFR 149.510).
Its out-of-network chapter treats leaving networks as a revenue choice. Omits the federal balance billing ban at in-network hospitals and the Medicare Advantage payment-in-full rule.

categories.evidence_note: Rules are set by statute and regulation: 38 U.S.C. 1703D and the Veterans Affairs claims guide, 32 CFR part 199 for the military plan, 45 CFR part 149 for surprise billing and estimates. In Florida, section 627.64194 adds a state ban. No benchmark exists.

metrics.name: Share of charges billed out of network
metrics.definition: Charges billed to payers with which the practice or the rendering clinician has no enrollment or contract, as a share of total charges.
metrics.formula: Charges to non-enrolled or non-contracted payers / total charges
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. Read it with the write-offs on those charges, which show what non-enrollment costs.
metrics.data_hint: Charges by payer against the enrollment tracker.
